Note: Posting on my Boyfriend's behalf as he played my copy of it. 

So, let me start off by saying this review's gonna contain MAJOR plot spoilers!  So, only read after you've played it.
Pre-spoiler: The game was good.  Leaves some room for improvement, but overall worth your time, at the very least.

****SPOILER STARTS NOW****



So, I'd say overall, I really did like this game.  The jumpscares are by far the worst part of it, as it's honestly the cheapest form of horror, but the atmosphere was built beautifully.  The actors did a great job making their acting believable.  Greg's actor started off sounding very off, but started getting more and more believable as the game went on.
As for the plot, it's very clearly inspired by stuff like Metal Gear Solid 2.  Though, admittedly it kinda blew the secret open from the very start, with the very first action by the player being to watch a video that kinda gives the twist away, unsubtly at that.  It was very obvious from the moment they started accusing each other that Greg and Taylor were red herrings, so it felt a little forced that I had to investigate both, even if I was given the opportunity to just believe them.
And, that leads me to the endings.  I got the "Abandon All Hope" ending, and haven't experienced the others, nor do I know what happens in them.  Honestly, I like the idea that no one will trust you if you don't trust them, but I'm not a huge fan of the game constantly hammering at me at the very ending that I fucked up.  Though, I do like the touch that the game conditions you early on to investigate everything, thus requiring some thought from the player to not keep doing that for everyone.
One last thing: I see your Telltale inspiration in telling you the major decision points and comparing it to everyone else's.  And, while it's a good way to keep track of what decisions were hard or easy to make, it kinda pulls the curtain away from how shallow the choice system is, basically telling the player all the choices that actually matter, and showing off just how binary they are.  Not saying you need to put hours of depth into literally hundreds of decisions, just saying showing the player a quantifiable chart of choices gives away the whole thing.

Overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth the $5 my boyfriend paid for it, and I can't wait to see more from this developer

A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it?

[h2] Story [/h2]
In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference. 

Some aspects were rewarding. I liked getting to put that one workplace creep in his place. I liked when I got her a new job in that one playthrough.

I think the main issues with the story were already discussed in the characters section. I don't think the payoff was satisfying. I think I see what they are going for, with the good ending that is. You have to become a master manipulator to take down the manipulator, I do like that. Again, I just felt like the final boss was an absolute joke. I thought it was fake, there was another boss behind the boss, or something. I think the plot excels in relationship drama and just making terrible people act terrible. It's guilty pleasure level entertaining. It gets lost in the big ideas and trying to be bigger than it actually is. I think if it had stuck to a nitty gritty found phone horror game, with people as its worst enemy, it would've stuck the landing a bit more.

[h2] Theme [/h2]
Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. 

Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna. 

[h1] Wait, didn't you recommend this game? I'm confused [/h1]
Yes. I do.

I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra wasn't an entirely bad experience. I actually had a decent time with most of the game. However, the overall package is important to me with a game. I only played through Mass Effect 3 once because the endings were so off-putting that I did not have any interest in playing through again because the conclusion lowered the quality of the game as a whole for me. Mind you, Simulacra doesn't have two games that came before it to ruin the legacy of or anything, nor is it even a tenth the length of Mass Effect 3, but an unsatisfying conclusion to any heavily story-focused game is often the ruin of many a game that were doing well up until that point.

With Simulacra, you navigate a missing girl's cell phone, using the text messaging, web browser, social media posts, and a dating app to further your investigation into where the girl is, gain a couple of allies to help with said investigation, and ultimately conclude with a villain which I won't spoil the identity of or anything like that. I will say that you should be able to easily understand a great villain when the villain monologues to you about why said villain is doing things, and there should be some logical explanations for the reasoning for the villain's actions, etc. Also, a villain shouldn't just pop out of nowhere, typically. Imagine if you got to the end of a deep storyline, and suddenly an extraterrestrial pops out without proper foreshadowing. It would make for a "good bad movie," but a terrible plot point. Again, I won't say specifics about this villain, but the villain does not seem to have a very logical viewpoint, and the villain pops practically out of nowhere and can do things that the game never explains which are vital to the main storyline.

Finally, there appear to be four different endings. Apparently the game locks you out of certain endings based on certain actions you take at some point in the game. I have no idea what those actions were or when they came up. Worse yet, there is no manual saving in Simulacra. There is ONE autosave file that overwrites every time you complete an objective, meaning to see the other endings, you have to start the game from the beginning again. The text messages pop up faster than before, but the game still takes too long for me to have the patience to play through it again, especially since the gameplay wasn't particularly enjoyable for me. Simulating a real cell phone was a cool premise, but it wasn't "fun" to interact with for me outside of the initial surprises of what the very small cast of characters (and an even smaller cast of *relevant* characters) have to say.

The ending I got was horribly dark and unpleasant, and the other ending that was offered to me was clearly going to be horribly dark and unpleasant as well. Dark endings can be entertaining if the storyline gives a satisfying quality to them that doesn't leave you feeling cheated. In Simulacra, the villain effectively tells you "lulz, you made decisions (that I'm not going to specify which ones or when) which set this stuff up. Now make horrible choice A, or horrible choice B." I stopped caring about the story immediately upon being given these options, and just proceeded to the ending knowing my conclusion was going to suck because I didn't play with a walkthrough and the game doesn't allow saving aside from the regularly-overwriting autosave, so you can't just load back a few minutes to make a different decision and see things play out differently.

Without very clear points of making relevant decisions, and without a manual save you can load, AND without enjoyable dark/"bad" endings, Simulacra left me disappointed in what initially seemed like a game I was going to talk about to others and say great things about it, but walling off endings sneakily and overwriting autosaves without a manual save option ruined the overall package of this game for me. I already regret the time I spent on it and I'm not going to waste any more of my time looking up the other endings online or replaying it. I will forever remember the crap ending choice the game locked me into and look back on Simulacra with disdain and disappointment.

I already own the sequel, Simulacra 2, but I no longer intend to play it because I dislike the first game so much now.

still definitely worth a playthrough!

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game [spoiler]Simulacra[/spoiler] would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.

Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris [spoiler]though of course allusions can be found in the website, thanks to the phone number and Morse Code[/spoiler], was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.

For the devs:
[list]
[*]The ambiance is brilliant.  I love the room behind the phone, the lights flickering and the sounds around me.  It definitely creates an aura of suspense.
[*]As far as jump scares, I agree with Night Mind, unnecessary, kind of lame, and ineffective.
[*]What did solving the puzzles accomplish?  I mean, I don't know if I had to unscramble the photos and texts to progress, I just always do it to get it out of the way, but they don't, in the story, progress anything, really, [spoiler]until the Spark conversation with James[/spoiler].  Also they were really easy.  When you present me with a four-word scramble...come on.
[*]Where is this supposed to take place?  The accents were peculiar.  It seemed like you were aiming for American, but you were using British spellings, i.e. favourite.  Is it meant to take place in Canada?
[*]I did love the multiple endings, and felt much more invested in them than I did in SiM.  In particular, [spoiler]I just achieved the happy ending, and afterward, stared at the screen and said, "Did I just get possessed?  I think I just got possessed."[/spoiler]
[*][spoiler]Even if you're interviewing through text (for reasons?), why would you consider hiring a person to be a copywriter who makes that many spelling and grammatical errors?  I kept looking at my response options, and they were painful.  Yes, I understand you're not really applying and just trying to get information about James, but still.[/spoiler]
[/list]
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if [spoiler]the final image had been the player lowering the screen and something vague and shadowy, or even a representation of the Simulacra, being there, and then moving toward the screen if you simply must jump scare, it would have been better than the shift in Anna's picture.[/spoiler]  It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.

Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

Unfortunately, Simulacra is just too poorly written to call it good. 
There are so many grammar and spelling issues throughout, then you throw in the frankly stupid direction the plot takes at a certain point (no spoilers) and it leaves you with an entirely underwhelming experience. 

On top of all that, the game effectively forces you into decisions that don't make sense if you want to get the good ending. 

If you're really into the idea of this game, you'd be better off with the mobile version. It's not written any better but it's more immersive. Some of the crappy jump-scares might actually get to you for a about 2 seconds that way.

review_text_raw:
Great idea, but bad execution. A for effort but C on the result.

PROS:
- Technical polish. The UI looks good and the videos, picture and audio are of good quality.
- The developers did seem to put their heart into this. It is not easy to make games involving so much detail, actors and voice work
- Interesting concept. While not original, piercing the story together through different apps on the phone was neat
- Some puzzles were neat like finding a phone number hidden in Twitter posts or creating a specific Tinder profile, because they fit the concept of the game really well

CONS:
- All the characters are downright unlikable.. I didn't care for Anna one bit and if there was an ending to kill them all off I would have took it. And when I mean all, I really mean all. Every single one, including her mother and the HR lady. I guess only the cat gets a pass and even then I'm not sure
- Unrealistic voice work. Most characters speak very unnaturally. The biggest offender being Greg who talks like he is in a kid's anime
- You can only speak to people when they are online, but they always pop up immediately when you need them to make progress, making it very obvious you are playing a videogame. A few seconds delay would have done wonders for the immersion
- Repetitive gameplay. Most of the time you will be doing the same "construct a phrase" or "remake a picture" puzzle and the whole cycle of restoring the phone data should have only happened once.
- Cheap cheap "horror" with zero atmosphere but instead lots of dumb jump-scares (really really a lot) and in-your-face weirdness. No subtlety whatsoever, making the "horror" cheap, pointless and braindead
- The ending. I felt dumber after the villain reveal and finished the game. Not sure I can put up with another run to see the other endings. I was expecting something stupid, but this worse than I expected

They really should have either cut the "horror" and gone full psychological crime thriller (which would have worked really well with the gameplay) or just go full ham and make the weirdness go on through the whole experience escalating more and more.
Instead you get a detective story ruined by awful jump scares or a horror story bogged down by boring detectice work. I would prefer the former as the later was really really bad, inspired by the worst horror movies the '10s had to offer.

I can forgive the bad dialogues and bad acting due to being an indie game, but I would suggest the developers to at least not use outdated memes in people's speech.

Only buy it on sale and expect a mediocre experience that pisses you off because it had the potential to be much better.

review_text_raw:
Summary: For a horror/mystery/puzzle game, it is quite weak on each of the three elements. The least surprising mystery game I've played. Perhaps mainly because it blows its load from the start and spends the rest of the play time catching up with itself. Probably works better on mobile, as it seems made for a short attention span.

Pros:
- Basic concept is a cool commentary on social media and online dating
- A couple of surprising moments
- Some easter eggs and alternative paths give a bit of replay value

Cons:
- Storytelling is overstated and predictable
- Dialog is unconvincing, and I often didn't like my choices
- Game is linear and holds your hand almost the entire way. Some light puzzles, but otherwise no challenge, except unlocking a certain ending
- Acting is meh, supporting voice acting is mostly plain bad
- Annoying spelling errors are not always intentional

For examples of similar storytelling that really works: see Oxenfree and Doki Doki Literature Club.

[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

review_text_raw:
Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.

You might think that this is a real-life mystery-horror thriller but no, you will find out that it is a B film in disguise - nonsensical plot, cringy acting, annoying jumpscares, and clichéd ending in one package!

The game was quite intriguing in the beginning. We have to use someone's phone to find out what happened to its owner. To my disappointment, the game got downhill fast.

Puzzles were OK, but watching the video messages was painful. If the devs didn't have enough fundings to hire good actors, then why not just leave out the video? They don't contribute to the plot anyway. There were also jumpscares, which were so out of place and annoying, all sense of immersion I had was ruined by them.

[spoiler]The worst was the ending. The villain was revealed to be an AI called Simulacra, who wanted to kill Anna because, in Simulacra's own words, she "is a worm in a perfect image that needs to be eradicated". Was this line supposed to be scary? Why does Simulacra speak like a cartoon villain?

The ending left me with more questions than answers. The biggest question is: How does an entity that only exists in the virtual space hijack people's bodies in real life?!?!?! Is there a Wi-Fi receiver in the human brain!? 

Even the story premise falls apart when you think about it: 
WHY did the villain/sockpuppet leave the phone on the player's doorstep in the first place?
If Simulacra could imitate other people in the cyberspace, then it could have just destroyed the phone and used Anna's identity to lure more victims online (indeed, at one point in the game Simulacra successfully wiped the phone data), instead of letting the player find out about Anna, who might then rescue her, or worse, warn everyone in the world about the existence of a cyberspace killer. On the topic of warning people, why didn't people who knew Anna contact the police instead of trying to solve the case on their own? When even an ordinary person realised that something fishy was going on, how come the police knew nothing about the disappearances when all the missing people had interacted with each other before they went missing? Did they not bother to do basic investigations?[/spoiler]

Finally, as a VN, being unable to manually save is unacceptable. You have to replay the game from the beginning to get an alternative ending.

It's a shame as this game had great potential to educate people about phone addiction and danger of social media.

review_text_raw:
A fun, innovative experience involving navigating someone’s digital life to find out what happened to someone.

Background: I like playing interactive stories like this while I’m eating instead of watching TV or a movie. It’s good to play these kinds of games between bites.

I didn’t know what to make of this game—I think I got it as part of a bundle—but installed it and tried it out after running through a few movie games and wanting to shift to something else. I was pleasantly surprised by the story, and the gameplay was similar to games like Her Story and Orwell where you interact with a digital interface to make the story unfold.

The Positives:
-It really does feel like you are a person who found a phone and are trying to find out what happened to the owner. There are a few times where it is imperfect in terms of what you probably could/should/would do, but it does a good enough job that it felt realistic enough to suspend disbelief for several hours.

-The phone was fun to play around with—you go into various apps and learn about the owner’s recent activity and then even get to participate a little.

-The people you interact with are sketchy as hell, but it definitely made things interesting.

-The ending got pretty wild; while the horror elements are minimal for most of the game, the ending combines the genres of tech-thrillers and evil-spirit-horror—very interesting. It’s not simply like System Shock 2 or Terminator (where the tech tries to control you) or Evil Dead or The Ring (where evil spirits are trying to kill you); it’s an interesting mix.

-The people involved did a great job—there are a lot of photos, videos, and conversations, and both the actors and the developers did a great job of making it all fit together. It all felt real—I never thought for a moment that the photos or videos were “fake” or “made-for-the-game”. That’s all I look for in acting; not everything has to be Meryl Streep, and this felt real enough.

-The ending was fresh for me—the combination of it being just slightly different from other endings in the genre along with the uniqueness of me having to make decisions that led to the outcome made the experience very new and interesting.

The Negatives:
-As I mentioned, the people you interact with are sketchy, which I overall enjoyed but it does result in some weird interactions. I thought it worked, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you played and said, “Why don’t they just do X?” — I felt that any plot holes were covered up well enough for me to buy it, but you might not.

-If you like a lot of horror, there isn’t much here—it ratchets up near the end but for the most part is more of a mystery with a dash of spooky/thriller elements. I liked the amount, but you might want more.

-It’s tough to strike a balance between elements that build the character and world with ones that begin to give you hints about the mystery…I think they did a good job, but you might find that early on you go through a lot of videos and photos that don’t reveal much. The photos are easy enough to skim through, but you’ll watch several videos and they don’t really do much other than give you a live look at what the owner looked like while slowly introducing the fact that something is amiss. If you’re a narrative critic, you’d probably want them to have done more with those elements than just a look into the life of the owner.

Overall, it’s an interesting game. I was engaged most of the time and there are only brief periods where there is a lot of text back-and-forth that you might want something more to be happening—but it’s not bad by any means. If you are sucked in at those points, you will enjoy it. If not, that’s probably where you might tune out. The good news is that the developers listened and put in the ability to adjust the speed, etc. of the game (especially if you’re replaying it) to solve for that issue. So I think you’ll be okay. As long as you like the mysterious look-into-the-life-of-someone-else genre of point-and-click games (like the “found footage” genre of movies but for video games), you’ll enjoy it. If you are hoping for a lot of horror, though, there isn’t too much and so I just hope to set your expectations appropriately.

[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. If you have ever wondered how ugly it could get in the event that AI were to take over, well, this game depicts one possible reality. 

Enjoyed it overall, but aiming to reach 100% completion left me with mixed feelings.


Simulacra is a modern take on a philosophical idea that originated in an essay called "Simulacra and Simulation" from 1981. It's simple, and yet, if you manage to reach any ending, and the true ending especially, you will likely ask yourself questions about how you approach your existence in our digitalised world.

The game has its flaws, but if you're okay with this format, then you will probably have a good time.


When I played Simulacra for the first time in 2018, I played it, and I enjoyed it a lot. I was impressed by the simplistic yet effective nature of the storytelling that was made relevant due to the then technologically transitional period: everyone learning how to use smartphones for almost anything. I also appreciated how little the game requires of you, safe for the patience to read, comprehend, observe, and stop to think for a moment, making it an easy recommendation for playing after a mentally and physically demanding day.

That was then. But what about now...?


Lately, I had been thinking a lot about the topics of Simulacra, Simulation, Simulacrum, and AI, so I decided to replay the game and complete it because I liked it so much my first time. It took me 2 playthroughs to reach completion. The first one took 4-5 hours, and the second - no more than 2-3. My recommendation if you were to seek completion within the day would be to do it with a guide next to you. Some achievements, especially the hidden one and the true ending, require noticing and doing a number of things, which could take you hours to nail by going back again and again -- which could be enjoyable if you're into that and are okay with spending more time with the game.

And here is a thing you'll wish to keep in mind: to reach 100% completion, you will need to open the corresponding save file folder, and create multiple backups (ideally, giving yourself context because it gets hard to make out the saves), because you will need to go back if you don't want to replay the game 5 or 6 times. Most of all, the save files will help you in the event that the game bugs out, as it tends to do -- for instance, when you use your keyboard to input something, and then press Enter, the game crashes; for others, some chats don't load properly; for others yet, some achievements refuse to pop up on the first or second try; and so on.


Do your due diligence to find out what's needed for 100% completion. I used Naps' guide on PlayStationTrophies.org, and made plenty of back up saves along the way. Feel free to comment if you need the files for your run, though imo it's more fun to do it along the way.

I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

This game is a bit annoying. I kinda enjoyed my time with it but it's just not good.

On the plus side: it's got decent social media puzzles and a sufficiently creepy atmosphere, ... and that's about all it has going for it. On the minus side: The writing is terrible, the voice acting is not great, there are several cheap jump scares, and the story itself is awful.

Ooh, the story has multiple endings and I should play again? No thank you, once is enough. I can't see what the game could have to offer besides more weak dialogue and weird railroady decisions.

Spoilers, I guess, but I lost and got the worst ending because I didn't show enough trust in the sleazebag (who was specifically written as a sleazy dude) ALL THE WAY IN THE BEGINNING OF THE GAME. It always bunches my britches when a game does that: "Oh you didn't do a thing when you didn't have all the information yet and you couldn't make an informed decision about it? Sucks to be you, Anna's dead." Oh, and also Taylor, he's dead too. Just because I wouldn't send the sleazy dude a cute selfie of the missing girl and I wasn't sufficiently sad enough about him being caught with his pants down (literally, fuck, it's such a contrived story).

I feel like the game is less about saving Anna and more about how you're supposed to protect the feelings of the two douchebag brodudes. There's only one other recurring character, Anna's best friend, Ashley, who could have been of great help, but the story sidelines her almost immediately and only brings her back to intimate that she's secretly in love with Anna. Again, spoilers, but if you've read this far, I doubt you care. (edit: Reading someone else's review, I just learned that to get the absolute best ending, you have to catfish the best friend and reciprocate her feelings without Anna's consent or Ashley's knowledge. Cool game, bro!)

Anyway, don't bother with this game unless you really want a 5 hour puzzle game with a crappy story.

[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" + multiple Endings, somewhat of replayability (though not much)

+ some interesting charachters, an unknown protagonist, possible similarities to real live 
   dating crimes (educational)

+ some interesting Achievements in and outside of the main story line

+ nice positive review link @ the end if you liked the game & none if you click on didn't like it^^

  mostly you get like 3 Dialog options for chats etc., but in most cases it will all result in the same, maybe one 
  added sentence or a word or two changed and stuff like that


All in all I do recommend it to anyone who likes FMV / interactive and/or invesitgative / mystery Genre games.

review_text_raw:
The story was nothing if not cliché. The concept of a found phone game is cool, or perhaps was at the time of release, but everything else surrounding this concept left me quite underwhelmed.

So many of the characters are creeps, and I find out I got the bad ending for not helping out either of the creeps continue their creep life.
This game also falls into the pitfall of any visual novel type game, it feels stricly linear and there doesn't feel like theres much you can do to change the outcome of the game. Of course this isn't entirely true; there are mutliple endings. But the steps you have to take to get the endings are either vague or require you to work with the aforementioned creeps to save a woman who shouldn't be placed in these creeps crosshairs.

Also what's the message of this game, that putting on an online persona is bad? Sure, maybe, but we see one character using a persona to her benefit?
Is it that forming relationships online is bad? Sure, they can be. But again; there are benefits to forming relationships online too.

The main villian of the game, if you could call it that, doesn't really have a solid theme. Is it AI? Something paranormal? Eldritch horror? A mix of them all plus more?
Even with this in mind, why make it a supernatural entity? Why can't the villian just be a normal guy, like what happens in real life. It feels like meta commentary for meta commentary sake. 

This is the kind of game I suspect would do well in a youtuber letsplay, it's something to be watched and commentated on. I suspect this because I only really had fun with this game because I was playing it with my friends.

As for the "horror" aspect, its a bit of a joke. Loud noises or random unexpected noises playing at random times - most egregiously "door knocking sfx"

Wouldn't reccomend, but its cheap so do as you will.
